nodes.name: Shannon's First Theorem
nodes.statement: $\lim_{m \to \infty} L_m / n = H(S)$; equivalently $n H(S) \leq L_m \leq n H(S) + 1$.
nodes.statement_clean: The minimum average number of bits to describe one symbol output by source $S$ equals $H(S)$.
assumptions: $S$ is a source over an alphabet $\Sigma$ with probability density $p$
$L_m$ is the minimum expected number of bits $A$ has to send to communicate $m$ output symbols of $S$ to $B$

nodes.name: Computationally infeasible Shannon-optimal coding
nodes.statement: Let $\Sigma$ be the set of all $k$-bit binary strings with $k = 10^4$; for 100-bit $x,m$ let $\alpha_{x,m}=c_1c_2\dots c_k$ where $c_j$ is the parity of $(x^j \bmod m)$, and let source $S$ have uniform distribution on $\Lambda \subseteq \Sigma$ of size $|\Lambda|=2^{200}$. Then $H(S) \leq 200$, but recovering $(x,m)$ from $\alpha_{x,m}$ may be computationally infeasible.
nodes.statement_clean: A source whose Shannon entropy is small but which apparently cannot be encoded efficiently in any feasible computation, motivating effective entropy.

nodes.name: Shannon's Second Theorem
nodes.statement: For any $R < \mathrm{capacity}(C)$ and $\epsilon > 0$, there exists (for sufficiently large $m$) a code $E$ of length $m$ and decoding rule $f$ such that (a) $|E| \geq 2^{Rm}$ and (b) $P(x) < \epsilon$ for all $x \in E$.
nodes.statement_clean: Channel $C$ can reliably transmit at any rate below its capacity.
assumptions: $C$ is a channel with input/output alphabets $I,J$ and capacity $\mathrm{capacity}(C) = 1 - q\log_2(1/q) - (1-q)\log_2(1/(1-q))$
conclusions: A code $E$ of length $m$ with $|E| \geq 2^{Rm}$ and per-codeword error $< \epsilon$ exists for all sufficiently large $m$

nodes.name: Source
nodes.statement: A $\textit{source}$ $S$ is a probability distribution $p$ over $\Sigma^{+}$ with finite expected length $\beta(S) = \sum_x p(x)|x|$.

nodes.name: Source ensemble
nodes.statement: A $\textit{source ensemble}$ $S$ is a sequence of sources $S_1, S_2, \dots$ with probability distributions $p_1, p_2, \dots$ such that for some fixed $t_2 > t_1 > 0$, $p_n(y) > 0$ implies $n^{t_1} < |y| < n^{t_2}$.

nodes.name: $(t,k)$-encoding
nodes.statement: A $(t,k)$-encoding of $S$ is a triplet of probabilistic algorithms $\mathcal{M}=(M_A,M_B,M_C)$ such that: (a) on input $\alpha=(n,x_1,\dots,x_{n^k})$ with $p_n(x_i)>0$, $M_A$ halts in time $O(n^t)$ producing output string $\beta$ with distribution $q_n(\alpha)$; (b) given $(n,\beta)$ from $q(\alpha)$, $M_B$ halts in time $O(n^t)$ and recovers $\alpha$ with probability $1 - O(v(n))$; (c) for $b > 0$ and any $\beta=\beta_1\dots\beta_u$ with each $\beta_i$ a possible output of $M_A$ for some $\alpha_i$ and $u=O(n^b)$, $M_C$ halts in $O(n^{b'})$ and outputs $\beta_1,\dots,\beta_u$ correctly with error $O(v(n))$.
nodes.statement_clean: A polynomial-time encoding/decoding scheme with uniquely decipherable codewords for blocks of $n^k$ source outputs.

nodes.name: $(t,k)$-entropy sequence
nodes.statement: A $(t,k)$-entropy sequence for $S$ is a sequence $w_1,w_2,\dots$ such that there exists a $(t,k)$-encoding $\mathcal{M}$ for $S$ with $L_n(\mathcal{M};S)=w_n$.

nodes.name: Effective entropy $H_e(S)$
nodes.statement: The effective entropy of $S$ is less than $g(n)$, written $H_e(S) \leq g(n)$, if for every fixed $t,k > 0$ there exists a $(t,k)$-entropy sequence $\{w_n\}$ for $S$ with $w_n \leq g(n)$ for all sufficiently large $n$. Symmetric notation $H_e(S) \geq h(n)$ defined analogously.

nodes.name: True random number ensemble $T_0$
nodes.statement: $T_0$ is the source ensemble $S_1,S_2,\dots$ where $S_n$ is defined by $p_n(x) = 2^{-n}$ if $|x|=n$ and $0$ otherwise.

nodes.name: Effective entropy lower bound (Theorem 1)
nodes.statement: For any source ensemble $S$, $H_e(S; n) \geq H(S_n) + O(v(n))$.
nodes.statement_clean: Effective entropy is at least the Shannon entropy (up to negligible terms).

nodes.name: Source with effective entropy far above Shannon entropy
nodes.statement: For any monotonic $g(n) \to \infty$ with $(\log_2 n)^2 < g(n) < n$, there is a source ensemble $S_n$ with $H(S_n) = g(n)$ but $H_e(S;n) = n + O(v(n))$. Construction: pick $\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\dots$ with $\alpha_n$ of length $n \cdot 2^{g(n)}$ and maximum Kolmogorov-Chaitin information; let $G(n)=2^{g(n)}$ and set $\alpha_n = \alpha_{n1}\dots\alpha_{nG(n)}$ with $|\alpha_{ni}|=n$; define $p(x)=2^{-g(n)}$ if $x=\alpha_{ni}$, else $0$.
nodes.statement_clean: There exist source ensembles whose effective entropy is much larger than their Shannon entropy.

nodes.name: $(t,k)$-coding scheme over channel $C$
nodes.statement: Let $S=(S_n)$ be a source ensemble and $C$ a channel with input/output alphabets $I,J$. A $(t,k)$-coding scheme of $S$ over $C$ is a triplet of probabilistic algorithms $\mathcal{M}=(M_A,M_B,M_C)$ that always halt in polynomial time $O(n^t)$, where $M_A$ encodes $\beta \in I^*$ from $n^k$ outputs of $S_n$, sends $\beta$ across $C$, $M_B$ decodes the channel output $\gamma \in J^*$ to $\delta$ with $\delta \neq \alpha$ of probability $O(v(n))$, and channel outputs are uniquely decipherable by $M_C$.

nodes.name: Expected channel cost $L_n(\mathcal{M}; S; C)$
nodes.statement: $L_n(\mathcal{M}; S; C)$ denotes the expected value of $|\beta|/n^k$ when input $\alpha$ to $M_A$ is generated probabilistically by $S_n$. The natural rate is $R_n = H_e(S;n) / [L_n(\mathcal{M};S;C)]$ fbits per channel transition.

nodes.name: Effective Shannon Second Theorem (Theorem 2)
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{M}$ be an encoding scheme for source ensemble $S$ over channel $C$. For any fixed $\epsilon > 0$, there exists an entropy sequence $\{w_m\}$ for $S$ such that $w_m < (\mathrm{capacity}(C) + \epsilon)\, L_n(\mathcal{M};S;C)$ for all sufficiently large $n$.
nodes.statement_clean: Any reliable encoding scheme over channel $C$ achieves effective rate at most $\mathrm{capacity}(C)$.
conclusions: There exists $(t,k)$-entropy sequence $\{w_m\}$ for $S$ with $w_m < (\mathrm{capacity}(C)+\epsilon)\, L_n(\mathcal{M};S;C)$ for all sufficiently large $n$

nodes.name: Lower bound on channel cost
nodes.statement: If $H_e(S;n) \geq h(n)$, then $L_n(\mathcal{M};S;C) > h(n) / (\mathrm{capacity}(C) + \epsilon)$ for all sufficiently large $n$.

nodes.name: Witness algorithm for $(S, S')$
nodes.statement: A witness algorithm $M$ for source ensembles $S=(S_n), S'=(S'_n)$ is a probabilistic algorithm such that for some $t,k$ and $\epsilon > 0$: (a) on input $(n,\alpha)$ with $\alpha \in (\Sigma^*)^{n^k}$, $M$ halts in time $O(n^t)$ with boolean output $M(n,\alpha)$, with $f_n(M,S) = \Pr[M(n,\alpha)=1]$ when $\alpha$ generated by $S_n$; (b) similarly $f_n(M,S')$ for $S'$; (c) there exists infinite $\{n_1,n_2,\dots\}$ with $|f_n(M,S) - f_n(M,S')| > \epsilon$ for $n=n_1,n_2,\dots$.

nodes.name: Indistinguishable source ensembles
nodes.statement: Two source ensembles $S$ and $S'$ are indistinguishable if there exists no witness algorithm for $S$ and $S'$.

nodes.name: Uniform source ensemble
nodes.statement: A source ensemble $S=(p_n)$ is uniform if all strings $x$ with $p_n(x)>0$ have the same length $\xi(n)$ and $\xi(n) < \xi(n+1)$ for all $n$. Call $\xi(n)$ the length function for $S$. $T_\xi$ is the source ensemble of $\xi(n)$-bit random numbers.

nodes.name: Perfect uniform source ensemble
nodes.statement: A uniform source ensemble $S$ with length function $\xi(n)$ is perfect if $S$ and $T_\xi$ are indistinguishable.

nodes.name: Polynomial statistical test
nodes.statement: A polynomial statistical test is a probabilistic algorithm $M$ that takes inputs $(x_1,\dots,x_{N^k})$ where each $x_i$ is an $N$-bit number, halts in time $O(N^t)$, and outputs a binary string $y$, where $t,k$ are fixed positive integers.

nodes.name: Passing a statistical test
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a polynomial statistical test and $S$ a uniform source ensemble. Then $S$ passes the statistical test $M$ if $\eta_M(N,y;S) - \eta_M(N,y) = O(v(N))$ for all $y$, where $\eta_M(N,y;S) = \Pr[\text{output } y \mid x_i \sim S_n,\, N=\xi(n)]$ and $\eta_M(N,y)$ is the analogous probability for inputs from $T_\xi$.

nodes.name: Statistical-test characterization of perfectness (Theorem 3)
nodes.statement: A uniform source ensemble $S$ is perfect if and only if $S$ passes every polynomial statistical test.
nodes.statement_clean: Perfectness (computational indistinguishability from true random) coincides with passing every poly-time statistical test.
conclusions: $S$ is perfect iff $S$ passes every polynomial statistical test

nodes.name: Information-theoretic characterization of perfectness (Theorem 4)
nodes.statement: A uniform source ensemble $S$ is perfect if and only if $H_e(S;n) = n + O(v(n))$.
nodes.statement_clean: Perfectness coincides with effective entropy equaling the maximum (for $n$-bit strings).
assumptions: $S$ is a uniform source ensemble (with length function $\xi(n) = n$ for simplicity)

nodes.name: Pseudorandom number generator
nodes.statement: A pseudorandom number generator $G$ is a probabilistic algorithm such that, given input integers $k$ and $n$: (a) halts in polynomial time in $n$, (b) uses $O(n)$ true random bits, (c) outputs a binary string $\alpha$ of length $n^k$.

nodes.name: Perfect pseudorandom number generator
nodes.statement: A pseudorandom number generator $G$ is perfect if for each $k$, the source ensemble $\mathcal{W}_k(G) = (S_n)$ where $S_n$ outputs $\alpha$ with the same probability $G$ does on input $(k,n)$ is a perfect uniform source ensemble.

nodes.name: Effective conditional-entropy notation $H_C(X|Y)$
nodes.statement: A $(t,k)$-encoding of $X$ relative to $Y$ is a triplet $\mathcal{M}=(M_A,M_B,M_C)$, where $M_A$ takes $\alpha=(n,x_1,\dots,x_{n^k},y_1,\dots,y_{n^k})$ and computes $\beta$ which together with $n$ and $y_1,\dots,y_{n^k}$ allows $M_B$ to recover $x_1,\dots,x_{n^k}$ with error $O(v(n))$; $M_A,M_B,M_C$ all halt in $O(n^t)$. $L_n(\mathcal{M};X|Y)$ is the average bits to encode a value $x$ of $X$. Notation: $H_C(X_n|Y_n) \leq g(n)$, $H_C(X_n|Y_n) \geq g(n)+O(h(n))$, etc., defined analogously to Definition 4.

nodes.name: Effective mutual information $I_C(X|Y)$
nodes.statement: Let $g(n),h(n)$ be any functions. Write $I_C(X_n|Y_n) \leq g(n)$ if for any conditional-entropy sequence $\{w_n\}$ for $X|Y$ there exists an entropy sequence $\{w'_n\}$ for $X$ with $w'_n \leq w_n + g(n)$ for all sufficiently large $n$. Expressions $I_C(X_n|Y_n) = O(v(n))$, $I_C(X_n|Y_n) \geq h(n)$, etc., similarly defined.

nodes.name: Symmetric effective independence (Theorem 5)
nodes.statement: $I_C(X_n|Y_n) = O(v(n))$ if and only if $I_C(Y_n|X_n) = O(v(n))$.
nodes.statement_clean: Effective mutual information vanishes symmetrically (in the small-information regime).
assumptions: $X,Y$ are random variables on a source ensemble $S$

nodes.name: Effectively independent random variables
nodes.statement: $X$ and $Y$ are said to be effectively independent if $I_C(X_n|Y_n) = O(v(n))$.

nodes.name: Independence via indistinguishability (Theorem 6)
nodes.statement: Let $X,Y$ be random variables on source ensemble $S$. Then $X,Y$ are effectively independent if and only if $S(X+Y)$ and $S(X \times Y)$ are indistinguishable, where $S' = S(X+Y)$ outputs $(x,y) = (X(\alpha), Y(\alpha))$ from a single $\alpha \sim S_n$, and $S'' = S(X \times Y)$ outputs $(x,y) = (X(\alpha_1), Y(\alpha_2))$ from independent $\alpha_1,\alpha_2 \sim S_n$.
nodes.statement_clean: Effective independence equates to computational indistinguishability of joint vs. product source.
assumptions: $X,Y$ random variables on a source ensemble $S$

nodes.name: Computational security of cryptosystem
nodes.statement: Consider users $A,B$ with secret key $K$ in keyspace, encryption $E(K,M)$, decryption $D(K,M)$, and ciphertext $J = E(K,M)$. Define source ensemble $Q = (Q_n)$ with $p_n(K_n=k) \cdot q_n(M_n=m)$. The cryptosystem is computationally secure if $H_C(M) \approx H_C(M|J)$, equivalently $I_C(M_n|J_n) = O(v(n))$. That is, $M$ and $J$ are computationally independent.

nodes.name: Trapdoor function (informal)
nodes.statement: A trapdoor function is a function $E_{K_A}$ where (a) given $K_A,x$, $E_{K_A}(x)$ is easy to compute; (b) given $K'_A,y$, $D_{K'_A}(y)$ is easy to compute; (c) given $E_{K_A}(x)$ alone it is computationally difficult to find $x$; (d) random pairs $(K_A, K'_A)$ are easy to generate.

nodes.name: RSA scheme
nodes.statement: User $A$ generates two random primes $p,q$ and integer $s$ with $\gcd(s,\phi(N))=1$ where $N=pq$ and $\phi(N)$ is Euler's totient. Public key $K_A=(N,s)$ and $r = s^{-1} \bmod \phi(N)$ is the private key $K'_A$. Encryption: $E_{K_A}(x) = x^s \bmod N$. Decryption: $D_{K'_A}(x) = x^r \bmod N$.
nodes.statement_clean: The RSA construction of a trapdoor function based on factoring.

nodes.name: Rabin's quadratic-residue trapdoor
nodes.statement: Define $E_{K_A}(x) = x^2 \bmod N$. Decryption is easy for $A$ who knows the factorization of $N$. Successful inversion of $E_{K_A}$ for any $\epsilon$ fraction of $x$'s enables factoring $N$ in random polynomial time.

nodes.name: Goldwasser-Micali probabilistic encryption (quadratic-residuosity)
nodes.statement: User $A$ generates random $n$-bit composite $N=pq$ and puts $N$ together with a non-residue $y \in A^*_N$ in the public file. To send bit $b$ to $A$, $B$ randomly generates $x \in Z^*_N$ and sends $x^2 \bmod N$ if $b=0$, $yx^2 \bmod N$ if $b=1$. $A$ can decide $b$ by deciding whether the received number is a quadratic residue.

nodes.name: Quadratic-residuosity circuit complexity $C_{n,\epsilon}$
nodes.statement: $C_{n,\epsilon}$ is the minimum size of any circuit that decides quadratic residuosity mod $N$ for a fraction $\epsilon$ of all $n$-bit integers $N$ with two prime factors.

nodes.name: Assumption GM
nodes.statement: $C_{n,\epsilon} > Q(n)$ asymptotically for any fixed polynomial $Q$ and any fixed $0 < \epsilon < 1$.

nodes.name: Discrete-logarithm circuit complexity $I_{m,\epsilon}$
nodes.statement: Let $p$ be a prime, $g$ a generator of the cyclic multiplicative group $A_p = \{1,2,\dots,p-1\}$. For $y \in A_p$ let $f(p,g,y)$ be the $x \in A_p$ such that $g^x \bmod p = y$. A boolean circuit with three $n$-bit inputs $a,b,c$ is said to solve the discrete logarithm problem for $p$ if its output is $f(p,g,y)$ when $a=p,b=g,c=y$. $I_{m,\epsilon}$ is the minimum size of any circuit solving discrete log for a fraction $\epsilon$ of all $n$-bit primes $p$.

nodes.name: Assumption BM
nodes.statement: $I_{m,\epsilon} > Q(n)$ asymptotically for any fixed polynomial $Q$ and any fixed $0 < \epsilon < 1$.

nodes.name: Polynomial-time distribution ensemble
nodes.statement: Let $P=(p_n)$ be a sequence of probability distributions on $\Sigma^+$ where the support of $p_n$ consists of strings of length $\theta(n)$. Call $P$ a polynomial-time distribution ensemble if there exists a probabilistic algorithm which on input $n$ halts in polynomial time and outputs $x$ with distribution $h(x)$ satisfying $\|h - p_n\| = O(v(n))$, where $\|h - p_n\| = \sum_x |h(x) - p_n(x)|$.

nodes.name: Correlation ensemble $Q^{f,P}$
nodes.statement: Let $f: V \to \Sigma^*$ be a 1-1 function, $P=(p_n)$ a polynomial-time distribution ensemble with support of every $p_n$ a subset of $V$. Define correlation ensemble $Q^{f,P} = (Q_n)$ where $Q_n = (T,q_n)$ has sample space $T = \{(x,f(x)) \mid x \in V\}$ and $q_n(\tau) = p_n(x)$ for $\tau = (x,f(x))$. Random variables $X^{f,P}_n = (X_n) = x$ and $Y^{f,P}_n = (Y_n) = f(x)$.

nodes.name: One-way function (Definition 22)
nodes.statement: A 1-1 function $f$ is one-way if there exists a polynomial-time distribution ensemble $P$ such that $H_C(X^{f,P}_n | Y^{f,P}_n) = \Omega(1/n^t)$ for some fixed $t$.
nodes.statement_clean: $f$ is one-way iff some fbits of information are needed to recover $x$ from $f(x)$ under the induced distribution.

nodes.name: Induced distribution $P^f$
nodes.statement: Let $f$ and $P$ be as in Definition 22. Define $P^f = (p^f_n)$ where $p^f_n(y) = p_n(f^{-1}(y))$.

nodes.name: Inversion characterization of one-wayness (Theorem 7)
nodes.statement: A 1-1 function $f$ is one-way if and only if there exists a polynomial-time distribution ensemble $P$ such that for any probabilistic algorithm which, on input $n$ and $y$ (with $y$ distributed according to $p^f_n$), halts in time polynomial in $n$ and outputs $x$, the probability of $x \neq f^{-1}(y)$ is $\Omega(1/n^t)$ for some fixed $t$.
nodes.statement_clean: $f$ is one-way iff no poly-time algorithm can invert $f$ with overwhelming probability under some efficiently sampleable distribution.
conclusions: $f$ is one-way iff there exists a polynomial-time distribution ensemble $P$ with the inversion lower bound holding

nodes.name: Stable one-way function (Definition 24)
nodes.section: Part 2, Sec 3 (One-way Functions with Invariance Properties)
nodes.statement: If in Definition 22 we also have $P^f = P$, then we call $f$ a stable one-way function.

nodes.name: Perfect PRG from stable one-way functions (Theorem 8)
nodes.statement: Any stable one-way function $f$ can be used to construct a perfect pseudorandom number generator $G_f$.
nodes.statement_clean: Stable one-way functions yield perfect PRGs.
conclusions: A perfect pseudorandom number generator $G_f$ is constructible from $f$

nodes.name: Computationally secure cryptosystem from stable one-way functions
nodes.statement: Any stable one-way function $f$ can be used to construct a computationally secure cryptosystem.
conclusions: A computationally secure cryptosystem (one-time-pad realization) is constructible from $f$

nodes.name: Discrete logarithm function
nodes.statement: Let $G_n = \{(p,g,m) \mid p \text{ is an } n\text{-bit prime}, g \text{ a generator of } A_p, m \in A_p\}$. Define $V = \bigcup_n G_n$ and $f: V \to V$ by $f(x) = (p,g,g^m \bmod p)$ if $x = (p,g,m)$. The key is $(p,g)$. Define $p^*_n(K) = 1/((\#\, n\text{-bit primes})\cdot(\#\,\text{generators in }A_p))$ if $K=(p,g)$ is possible, else $0$; $p^{**}_{n,K}(m) = 1/(p-1)$ if $m \in A_p$, else $0$; $p_n(x) = p^*_n(K) \cdot p^{**}_{n,K}(m)$.
nodes.statement_clean: The discrete-log function is a one-way function with a key under Assumption BM.

nodes.name: One-way function with a key (Definition 25)
nodes.statement: A one-way function $f$ has a key if the domain $V$ has the form $V \subseteq \Sigma_1^* \times \Sigma_2^*$ and there exists a polynomial-time distribution ensemble $P=(p_n)$ such that: (a) $P$ makes $f$ a one-way function as in Definition 22; (b) $p_n(x) = p^*_n(K) \cdot p^{**}_{n,K}(z)$ if $x=(K,z)$, where $(p^*_n)$ and $(p^{**}_{n,K})$ are polynomial-time distribution ensembles; (c) $f(x)$ can be written as $(K, f^*_K(z))$ for $x=(K,z)$.

nodes.name: Trapdoor function (formal sketch, Sec 4)
nodes.statement: A trapdoor function is essentially a one-way function with a key $K$ such that an inverse key $K'$ can be easily created at the same time, but $K'$ cannot be inferred from $K$. (Formal definition omitted in the abstract.)

nodes.name: Probabilistic public-key cryptosystem (PPKC)
nodes.statement: A probabilistic public-key cryptosystem is a cryptosystem in which user $A$ has an $n$-bit key $K$ in a public file while keeping a key $K'$ private. To send a bit $b \in \{0,1\}$, $B$ uses $b$ and $K$ to compute probabilistically a string $z$ and send it to $A$. The keys are generated such that, knowing $K'$, $A$ can uniquely recover $b$. A PPKC is secure if for $b$ with bias $p \geq 1/2$, an adversary cannot guess $b$ from $K$ and $z$ in polynomial time with probability more than $p + O(v(n))$.

nodes.name: Secure PPKC from any trapdoor function (Theorem 9)
nodes.statement: Any trapdoor function can be used to construct a secure PPKC.
nodes.statement_clean: Trapdoor functions imply secure probabilistic public-key cryptosystems (in general, not just for special structure).
conclusions: A secure PPKC is constructible from $f$

nodes.name: Intractability assumption of factoring
nodes.statement: For any polynomial-time probabilistic algorithm $M$ that tries to factor integers, there exists $n_0$ such that $M$ will fail to factor at least $1/n^{10}$ of the members of $T_n$ for all $n \geq n_0$, where $T_n$ is the set of $N = pq$ with $p \equiv q \equiv 3 \bmod 4$, $p,q$ both $n$-bit primes.

nodes.name: Factoring trapdoor function
nodes.statement: Generate $(K,K')$ by picking two random $n$-bit primes $p,q$ with $p \equiv q \equiv 3 \bmod 4$, set $K = N (= pq)$ and $K' = (p,q)$. Define trapdoor function $f$ by $f(N,x) = x^2 \bmod N$ if $x$ is even, $f(N,x) = -x^2 \bmod N$ if $x$ is odd, for $x \in A^*_N$.
nodes.statement_clean: A new factoring-based trapdoor function (a stable one-way function), distinct from RSA/Rabin.

nodes.name: Quadratic-residue pseudorandom number generator
nodes.section: Part 2, Sec 4 (A Quadratic-Residue Pseudorandom Number Generator)
nodes.statement: Generate a sequence $\beta$ of $n^k$ bits using $O(n(\log n)^2)$ true random bits via XOR of $t = (\log_2 n)^2$ quasi-random sequences, each obtained by squaring iteratively mod $N$ and reading the parity bit.
nodes.pseudocode: Procedure for one quasi-random sequence $\alpha$: pick random $N$ from $T_n$ and random $m$ with $1 \leq m \leq N-1$; compute sequence $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{n^k}$ by $x_1 = m$, $x_{i+1} = f(N, x_i)$; let $\alpha = \alpha_1 \alpha_2 \dots \alpha_{n^k}$ where $\alpha_i$ is the parity of $x_i$. Repeat to obtain $t = (\log_2 n)^2$ quasi-random strings $\alpha^{(1)}, \dots, \alpha^{(t)}$; output $\beta = \alpha^{(1)} \oplus \alpha^{(2)} \oplus \dots \oplus \alpha^{(t)}$.

nodes.name: Strong one-way function (Definition 26)
nodes.statement: $f$ is a strong one-way function if there exists $P$ such that $B_n(f,P) > Q(n)$ asymptotically for any polynomial $Q$, where $B_n(f,P)$ is the size of the smallest boolean circuit $C$ that inverts $f$ under $p_n$, with $C$ said to invert $f$ under $p_n$ if $\sum_{y \in T} p_n(y) > 1/2$ where $T$ is the set of input strings $y$ for which $C$ gives output $f^{-1}(y)$.

nodes.name: Strong one-way functions imply $R \subseteq \bigcap DTIME(2^{n^\epsilon})$ (Theorem 10)
nodes.statement: If there exists any strong one-way function, then $R \subseteq \bigcap_{\epsilon > 0} DTIME(2^{n^\epsilon})$.
nodes.statement_clean: Any strong one-way function gives a non-trivial deterministic simulation of randomized polynomial time.

nodes.name: Strong intractability assumption of factoring
nodes.statement: $F(n) > Q(n)$ asymptotically for any fixed polynomial $Q$, where $F(n)$ is the minimum size of any boolean circuit that can factor $4/5$ of the $2n$-bit composite numbers $N$ with two $n$-bit prime factors.

nodes.name: Corollary to Theorem 10 (factoring hardness implies $R \subseteq \bigcap DTIME$)
nodes.statement: Under the strong intractability assumption of factoring, $R \subseteq \bigcap_{\epsilon > 0} DTIME(2^{n^\epsilon})$.
assumptions: Strong intractability assumption of factoring holds

nodes.name: Discrete logarithm problem $D_{p,g}$
nodes.statement: Let $p$ be an $n$-bit prime and $g$ any generator of $A_p$. The discrete logarithm problem $D_{p,g}$ is: given input $y \in A_p$, find $x$ such that $g^x \bmod p = y$. Let $\ell(D_{p,g})$ be the minimum boolean circuit size for solving $D_{p,g}$. Define $L(n) = \max\{\ell(D_{p,g}) \mid \log_2(p+1) \leq n\}$.

nodes.name: Intractability assumption of discrete logarithm
nodes.statement: $L(n) > Q(n)$ asymptotically for any fixed polynomial $Q$.

nodes.name: Theorem 11 (discrete log intractability implies $R \subseteq \bigcap DTIME$)
nodes.statement: Under the intractability assumption of discrete logarithm, $R \subseteq \bigcap_{\epsilon > 0} DTIME(2^{n^\epsilon})$.

nodes.name: Theorem 12' (stronger derandomization from harder discrete log)
nodes.statement: If $L(n) > 2^{n^\epsilon}$ for some fixed $\epsilon > 0$ and for all $n$, then $R \subseteq DTIME(2^{(\log n)^c})$ for some constant $c > 0$.

nodes.name: Effective entropy as a sharpened information measure
nodes.statement: Property (c) of Definition 2 implies that codes are uniquely decipherable in the sense that to transmit $u \cdot n^k$ outputs of $S_n$, one can encode each $n^k$ segment separately and then concatenate the $u$ blocks for transmission. Thus we use the term 'effective entropy of a source ensemble' in the same spirit as 'computational complexity of a decision problem'.

nodes.name: Source-ensemble length restriction is non-essential
nodes.statement: The assumption $n^{t_1} < |y| < n^{t_2}$ in Definition 1 is not essential, but useful for simplifying later discussions; it is satisfied by most applications of interest.

nodes.name: Wyner wiretap analogy
nodes.statement: The role of $B$ as eavesdropper trying to wiretap a clear channel from $A$ to $G$ (the secret-key holder) with low-grade equipment is exactly analogous to the Wyner wiretap channel; trapdoor encoding magnifies the noise to baffle $B$ even when $B$'s noise is small (e.g. $n^{-\epsilon}$).

nodes.name: Sketch of Theorem 10
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a 1-1 onto function on a subset of $\{0,1\}^*$ and $P=(p_n)$ a polynomial-time distribution ensemble invariant under $f$. The proof leverages the fact that strong one-wayness imposes a circuit lower bound, which can be combined with the relation $R \subseteq \bigcap DTIME(2^{n^\epsilon})$ via simulation of random bits using $f$-iterates.
